How the algorithm works

We built the first pass to reduce uneven shading on scanned map paper. Reviewing its output revealed a remaining yellow cast, yellow fringes beside ink, and darker dots in areas that had been lightened. Each led to a separate correction. The tool estimates a fresh paper reference for each scan and applies the same rules automatically, without stain annotations, manual tuning, or model training.

  1. Estimate the paper color

    Sample bright, low-texture areas with relatively weak color. Follow connected pixels with similar colors to identify areas that are likely to be paper.

  2. Correct shading and broad stains

    Estimate gradual changes in brightness and color from those areas, then apply a limited correction at the original resolution. Check edges again before changing pixels near fine lines.

  3. Reduce the remaining yellow cast

    In areas already corrected, use the scan’s paper color to estimate how much blue is still missing. This step came from a Sacramento scan that remained yellow after brightening.

  4. Reduce halos along ink

    Use nearby corrected paper to estimate the adjustment for warm pixels beside a dark line. Apply it when their original color matches the surrounding paper and they are light enough.

  5. Reduce isolated brown spots

    Find compact dark, warm spots in the corrected image. Look for a ring of already corrected paper with similar original color. Apply and blend the adjustment away from dark ink.

  6. Repair dark spots from uneven correction

    Version 0.2.0 extends the correction across small gaps on similar paper and checks for excess contrast near each edit.

  7. Export a full-resolution PNG

    Save an RGB image at the source dimensions so the cleaned scan still aligns with the original.

Five archived v5 whole-map comparisons

We processed 37 distinct scans across development runs. The spot-correction experiment covered nine scans. The five maps below all show the v5 output alongside the original, with the scan edges visible.

A closer look at San Francisco Sheet 6

These crops compare the previous cleanup with the result after adding spot correction.

10 of 12 spots faded
In two Sheet 6 development crops, 10 sampled spots decreased in contrast by at least 2 units on the CIE76 color-distance scale.
24 print samples retained
Selected print areas on five other maps kept their original RGB values across all 168,802 sampled pixels.
5,805 × 8,268 pixels
The Sheet 6 PNG downloaded from the tool matched the offline output at the source resolution.

Deep marks, dense stains along the binding, and some gray specks remain visible. The Sheet 6 spots were used to develop the rule. Their results measure those selected locations.

Source scans from the Library of Congress, Geography and Map Division, Sanborn Maps Collection.
